intro.title: Edit Distance
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a function that calculates the edit distance (also known as Levenshtein distance) between two strings. The edit distance is the minimum number of single-character edits (insertions, deletions, or substitutions) required to change one string into another. You will learn to implement this using dynamic programming, a technique for solving complex problems by breaking them down into simpler overlapping subproblems. The main constructs involved include 2D arrays for storing intermediate results and nested loops to fill the array based on character comparisons. This exercise will help you understand how to apply dynamic programming to solve real-world string manipulation problems efficiently.
intro.usecase: Edit distance algorithms power spell-checkers in word processors and code editors by calculating how many changes are needed to transform a misspelled word into a correct one. They enable DNA sequence alignment in bioinformatics tools, helping researchers compare genetic codes. In version control systems like Git, they determine the minimal edits between file versions for efficient diff displays. These algorithms also enhance search engines by finding similar queries or autocorrecting typos in real-time.
